claims.statement: Attention is not a unitary salience response; top-down goals, bottom-up stimulus factors, and selection history interact and compete.

ANT network scores are not equally reliable; alerting and orienting difference scores have shown low split-half reliability relative to executive control, so ANT outputs cannot be treated as interchangeable high-precision trait measures.
Cultural meaning systems can alter object-versus-context allocation of visual attention, so attention effects should not be assumed culturally invariant.
Curiosity requires a multi-mechanism model including uncertainty, information gain, learning progress and exploration rather than a single information-gap rule.
Information avoidance is distinct from simply low curiosity or absent seeking; threat, self-beliefs, social factors and situational factors can motivate active avoidance of available information.
Trait curiosity is measurably multidimensional; CEI-II and 5DCR operationalize different facet structures rather than supporting one scalar curiosity variable.
Curiosity instruments have shown cross-cultural portability in specific samples, including Germany/UK and an Indonesian CEI-II adaptation, but this is not evidence of global invariance.
Subjective valuation and emotion are interacting but non-identical processes: affect can modulate value computation, and value-based decisions can incorporate affective reactions.
Appraisal-emotion relationships are differentiated across many appraisal dimensions and emotions rather than collapsing to one generic affective value signal.

Dimensional affect measures such as SAM and positive/negative affect instruments such as PANAS measure different affective representations and should not be used as a direct measurement of subjective value.
Cross-cultural emotion differences are partly substantive and partly methodological; culture and measurement method materially affect observed emotion differences.
Identity-based influence depends on self-categorization, group norms, identification and context rather than generic similarity.
Social identity and group identification are multidimensional; validated measures distinguish components such as self-definition, self-investment, membership esteem and importance to identity.

Cross-national measurement invariance of identity measures is imperfect; a 30-country analysis found noninvariance in a meaningful subset of parameters, particularly for some collective-interdependent items.
Experimental heuristic source/social cues produce a small-to-moderate average increase in perceived credibility, with source cues stronger than social cues and participant type acting as a moderator.
Perceived credibility is not equivalent to factual accuracy or calibrated trust; social/source cues can shift credibility judgments without verifying message truth.
Influencer credibility effects vary across methodological, geographic, platform, product and influencer contexts, so pooled effects are not universal runtime coefficients.
Parasocial interaction and parasocial relationship require distinct representation; modern PSR measurement is multidimensional and older online/offline scales are not automatically interchangeable.
Parasocial outcome associations vary by parasocial construct, age and cultural region, requiring developmental and cultural context in reasoning.
Parasocial engagement is not uniformly beneficial or harmful and its observed associations do not establish a universal causal connection-to-outcome pathway.

Social transmission has multiple drivers including impression management, accessibility, emotion regulation, information acquisition, social bonding and persuasion, while audience and communication medium moderate what is shared.

Stated willingness to share is an imperfect proxy for later real behavior; one prospective validation found only moderate correspondence and different determinants of intentions versus actual sharing.
Two preregistered replications found no effect of incidental physiological arousal on social-media sharing willingness, rejecting a universal arousal-to-sharing rule.
Culture and self-construal can shape communication and sharing behavior, while non-cultural platform and network factors also contribute.
Habit involves learned context-response control/automaticity and must be distinguished from mere repetition, goal intention and return behavior.
SRBAI is best interpreted as an automaticity index rather than a complete habit measure; self-report cannot fully identify context-specific cue-response associations.

Model-free reinforcement learning and habit are not interchangeable constructs; value-based learning can contribute to repeated control, but human habit can also be outcome-insensitive and frequency/context based.
Objective context-response and devaluation/frequency-based paradigms provide mechanistic information that self-report or returning-frequency metrics cannot supply.
